result: The study developed a novel Hierarchical Frequency Tagging (HFT) paradigm that combines SWIFT (1.3 Hz) and SSVEP (10 Hz) methods to simultaneously tag different levels of the visual hierarchy using scrambled face and house images.
evaluation: Claims C3, C12, C24, C27, C28, C124, and C125 collectively describe the methodological innovation. The experimental design is clearly documented with specific parameters (frequencies, image pools, scrambling methods), and Figure 1 provides visual evidence of the stimulus construction. The methods are sufficiently detailed for replication.

result: Significant frequency-tagged responses were observed at both fundamental tagging frequencies (f1=10 Hz, f2=1.3 Hz), their harmonics, and at various intermodulation (IM) components.
evaluation: Claims C29 and C30 report the basic frequency-tagging results shown in Figure 2. Statistical testing (one-sample t-test, FDR-adjusted p<0.01) supports the significance of peaks at both tagging frequencies and IM components. This demonstrates the technical success of the dual-tagging approach.

result: SSVEP signals showed strongest SNRs over occipital regions, SWIFT signals over temporo-parietal regions, and IM components over occipital regions. IM topography was significantly more correlated with SSVEP than SWIFT distribution.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 and C86 describe topographic findings shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. Statistical testing (Fisher's r-to-z transformation, z>5.5, p<0.01 for all IM components) supports the differential spatial distributions. The findings are consistent with prior literature (C35, C36) and predictive coding predictions (C37-C38).

result: SSVEP signals (10 Hz) were not significantly modulated by certainty levels, consistent with low-level visual processing that is unaffected by prediction strength.
evaluation: Claims C39, C40, C56 report the null effect of certainty on SSVEP shown in Figures 4 and 5A. Likelihood ratio tests with linear mixed models support this finding. Claim C41 provides a reasonable interpretation consistent with SSVEP reflecting bottom-up sensory input. The null result is appropriately interpreted rather than over-interpreted.

result: SWIFT signals (1.3 Hz) significantly decreased with increasing certainty, interpreted as reflecting reduced prediction error weighting under high certainty conditions.
evaluation: Claims C42, C57, C73 report the negative relationship between SWIFT and certainty shown in Figures 4 and 5B, supported by likelihood ratio tests (χ²=74.37, p<0.001). Claims C43, C44, C74 provide interpretations consistent with predictive coding theory. The interpretation is plausible but remains somewhat indirect as acknowledged by the authors.

result: Intermodulation (IM) signals increased with increasing certainty for three of four IM components, interpreted as reflecting enhanced integration between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory input when predictions are more certain.
evaluation: Claims C45, C46, C58, C89 report the positive relationship between IM and certainty shown in Figures 4 and 5C. Statistical testing supports the effect for three IM components (f1-2f2, f1-f2, f1+2f2) and across all four components combined (χ²=96.32, p<0.001). The interpretation (C47, C48) aligns with predictive coding predictions, though one IM component (f1+f2) did not show the effect, which is not fully explained.

result: The effect of certainty differed significantly across frequency categories, with IM showing a steeper positive slope than SSVEP, and SWIFT showing a negative slope compared to SSVEP.
evaluation: Claims C49 and C50 report significant interactions between certainty and frequency category supported by likelihood ratio tests (χ²=12.49 and χ²=64.45, both p<0.001). This demonstrates differential modulation of the three signal types by certainty, supporting the interpretation that they reflect distinct computational processes.

result: The HFT paradigm provides evidence that top-down predictions integrate with bottom-up sensory signals in a manner modulated by certainty, supporting predictive coding theories of perception.
evaluation: Claims C5, C116, C117 present the main conclusions. While the data show differential modulation of SSVEP, SWIFT, and IM by certainty (supported results above), the interpretation that these signals specifically reflect bottom-up input, top-down predictions, and their integration (C53, C54) remains indirect. Claims C84, C85 acknowledge this limitation. Alternative explanations (C101-C107) are considered but not definitively ruled out. The evidence is consistent with predictive coding but not uniquely diagnostic.

result: The decrease in SWIFT with certainty can be explained by either reduced prediction error signals or neural adaptation/repetition suppression, which are reconcilable under predictive coding frameworks.
evaluation: Claims C75-C80 discuss the interpretation of SWIFT findings in relation to prior literature on predictive stimuli and adaptation. The discussion appropriately cites relevant work (Alink et al., 2010; Todorovic et al., 2011; Auksztulewicz & Friston, 2016; Summerfield et al., 2008) and explains how adaptation can be understood within predictive coding. This represents a thoughtful integration with existing literature.

result: The study proposes a mapping of HFT components onto specific elements of predictive coding models, suggesting SWIFT and SSVEP may reflect conditional expectations of hidden causes and states, respectively, with IMs potentially encoding model evidence.
evaluation: Claims C95-C100 propose theoretical mappings to the Auksztulewicz & Friston (2016) model. While these mappings are conceptually plausible and consistent with the data, they remain speculative (C98 explicitly labeled as speculation). No quantitative predictions are tested, and the authors acknowledge this is an "interesting question for further research." The proposals are valuable for future work but not empirically validated here.

result: Alternative feedforward explanations for IM findings are considered but argued to be less parsimonious than top-down/bottom-up integration accounts, particularly given the differential modulation by certainty.
evaluation: Claims C101-C107 present and address alternative interpretations. The authors provide logical arguments (C102, C103) and cite relevant prior work (C104, C106) to argue against purely feedforward explanations. While alternatives cannot be definitively excluded (C105), the reasoning is sound and appropriately cautious. This represents good scientific practice in considering alternative explanations.

result: The study used implicit online learning of certainty levels rather than explicit cues, which may add uncontrolled variability but provides greater ecological validity.
evaluation: Claims C112-C115 discuss the certainty manipulation approach. The authors appropriately acknowledge both limitations (C114) and strengths (C115) of their design choice. This represents transparent reporting of methodological decisions and their implications. The trade-off between experimental control and ecological validity is explicitly recognized.

result: The study tested 27 participants, excluded 10 based on pre-defined criteria (5 for poor task performance, 5 for poor EEG quality), and analyzed data from 17 participants with 5.5% of trials excluded.
evaluation: Claims C126-C140 describe participant recruitment, exclusion criteria, and final sample. The exclusion criteria are clearly defined and justified (correlation r<0.9 for task performance; >10% noisy cycles for EEG quality). The final sample size (N=17) is within the typical range for SSVEP/SWIFT studies (C128). Exclusion rates are reasonable and transparently reported.

result: Certainty was manipulated by varying the proportion of face vs. house images across trials (50-100% of one image type), operationalized as 10 bins for analysis, while keeping stimulus precision constant.
evaluation: Claims C18, C20, C21, C26, C148, C149 describe the certainty manipulation. The design is clearly specified with proportion ranges and binning procedures. Claim C21 appropriately notes that stimulus precision (noise level) was held constant, isolating the manipulation to prediction precision. The operationalization is appropriate for testing predictive coding predictions.

result: Statistical analyses used FFT for frequency extraction, SNR for signal quantification, log2 transformation for normality, linear mixed-effects models with likelihood ratio tests, and FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
evaluation: Claims C141-C152 describe the statistical analysis pipeline. Methods are standard for frequency-tagging studies (FFT, SNR calculation per Srinivasan et al., 1999). The log2 transformation is justified (C146, C147). Mixed-effects models appropriately account for nested data structure. Multiple comparison correction (FDR) is applied. The analysis approach is rigorous and appropriate.

result: The manuscript provides background on predictive coding theory, including its historical development, core concepts (prediction errors, precision weighting, Bayesian inference), and empirical support from prior studies.
evaluation: Claims C1-C10 and C59-C68 present background knowledge about predictive coding, supported by extensive citations to relevant literature (Srinivasan et al., 1982; Rao & Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005; and many others). The background is accurate and appropriately cited. This provides necessary context for interpreting the current findings.

result: The manuscript describes SSVEP and SWIFT methods, their differential tagging of visual hierarchy levels, and the rationale for combining them in the HFT paradigm.
evaluation: Claims C11, C36, C52, C71, C72, C118-C123 describe the SSVEP and SWIFT methods with appropriate citations to prior work (Koenig-Robert & VanRullen, 2013; Koenig-Robert et al., 2015; Di Russo et al., 2007). The description accurately represents these methods and their properties. The rationale for combining them is clearly articulated.

result: Intermodulation components arise from nonlinear integration of signals at different frequencies, have been used in prior visual neuroscience studies, but cannot definitively identify specific computational processes.
evaluation: Claims C13-C15 and C82-C85 describe the intermodulation phenomenon and its application. The description is accurate and supported by citations (Clynes, 1961; Regan & Regan, 1988; Boremanse et al., 2013; Kouh & Poggio, 2008). The authors appropriately acknowledge (C84, C85) that IM presence alone doesn't uniquely identify mechanisms, showing appropriate scientific caution.

result: The manuscript provides theoretical background on expectation, certainty, and precision in predictive coding, supported by citations to relevant literature.
evaluation: Claims C16, C17, C19 describe theoretical concepts with appropriate citations (Summerfield & Egner, 2009; Kok et al., 2012a; Mathys et al., 2014). The theoretical framework is accurately represented and provides necessary context for the certainty manipulation.

result: Participants viewed 56 trials of 50-second movies containing face and house images at 1.3 Hz while counting presentations of one image type, with appropriate experimental controls (chin rest, viewing distance, dimly lit room).
evaluation: Claims C22, C23, C25, C130, C131 describe the experimental procedure. The task design is clearly specified with appropriate parameters. The counting task ensures attention to the stimuli. Experimental setup details (viewing distance, lighting) are provided. The procedure is adequately described for replication.

result: EEG data were acquired from 64 electrodes at 500-1000 Hz, preprocessed with high-pass filtering (0.6 Hz) and average referencing using EEGLAB.
evaluation: Claims C132-C136 describe data acquisition and preprocessing. Standard EEG methods are used with appropriate parameters. The use of EEGLAB (C134) is standard in the field. Preprocessing steps (filtering, referencing, resampling) are clearly documented. Methods are sufficient for replication.

result: Under predictive coding, predictions project to lower cortical levels for integration with sensory input, suggesting IM signals should localize to occipital regions and reflect integration efficacy.
evaluation: Claims C37, C38, C51, C81, C108-C110 present theoretical predictions and the rationale for the HFT approach. The reasoning is logically sound and consistent with predictive coding theory. The prediction about IM localization (C38) was confirmed by the data (C33). The claimed advantage of HFT over prior IM studies (C110) is reasonable.
